hints: Think about what any electrode potential must be measured against, since a single half-cell voltage cannot be measured on its own.
Recall the three standard condition values for ion concentration, gas pressure and temperature that make the $E$ value an $E^\ominus$ value.
walkthrough:
Picture what a half-cell voltage really means**
You can never dip a voltmeter into one beaker and read a voltage. A voltage is always a difference between two electrodes. So by definition every $E^\ominus$ is the voltage of your half-cell when it is connected to the agreed zero, which is the standard hydrogen electrode, $\text{Pt}|\text{H}_2|\text{H}^+$.

Add the three numbers that make it standard**
For the comparison to be fair, everything must be in its standard state. That means all aqueous ions at $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$, any gas at $101\ \text{kPa}$, and a temperature of $298\ \text{K}$. Quote all three to earn the second mark.

Final answer: The standard electrode potential is the voltage of a half-cell compared to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE).
Measured under standard conditions: $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for ions, $101\ \text{kPa}$ for gases, $298\ \text{K}$.

hints: Start with the half-cell you are testing: what metal and what solution must be in contact for $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})/\text{Ag}(\text{s})$?
Recall the full contents of the other half-cell, the SHE: which metal, which gas delivery and which acid are needed?
Think how the two beakers are joined electrically without mixing, and how the voltage is read between the two metals.
walkthrough:
Build the silver side**
The $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})/\text{Ag}(\text{s})$ half-cell is simple because silver is a metal conductor. Put an $\text{Ag}$ rod directly into a solution containing $\text{Ag}^+$, for example $\text{AgNO}_3(\text{aq})$. No platinum is needed here.

Build the hydrogen side**
The SHE needs an inert platinum electrode because there is no metal in the $\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2$ couple to conduct. Bubble $\text{H}_2$ gas over the $\text{Pt}$ foil dipping into $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$, for example $\text{HCl}(\text{aq})$, using a gas inlet tube.

Complete the circuit correctly**
Join the two electrolytes with a salt bridge, often filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_3(\text{aq})$, to allow ion flow. Join the two metals with wires through a high resistance voltmeter, $\text{Pt}$ to voltmeter to $\text{Ag}$, so no current is drawn.

Final answer: Left beaker (SHE): Pt electrode with $\text{H}_2$ gas bubbled over it in $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$. Right beaker: Ag electrode in $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})$. The two solutions joined by a salt bridge, the two metals joined via a voltmeter with wires Pt to voltmeter to Ag.

hints: Write the reduction equilibrium $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}(\text{s})$ and ask which way Le Chatelier shifts it if $[\text{Ag}^+]$ is lowered.
walkthrough:
Use Le Chatelier on the half equation**
Think of $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}(\text{s})$ as a dynamic equilibrium. Lowering $[\text{Ag}^+]$ removes reactant, so the system shifts left to try to replace it. Reduction is less favoured, the electrode is less easily reduced, so the electrode potential $E$ moves to a more negative value compared with $E^\ominus$.
Final answer: $E$ becomes more negative / less positive than $E^\ominus$ because the equilibrium $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}(\text{s})$ shifts to the left.

hints: Focus on the words dissolve and water: what starting amount and what final state define $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^\ominus$?
walkthrough:
Say exactly what dissolves and how much**
$\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^\ominus$ is not about melting or reacting. It is the heat change when $1$ mole of a solid solute spreads out into water to give aqueous ions, $\text{MX}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{M}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{X}^-(\text{aq})$. Just state one mole dissolving in water.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves in water / to form an infinitely dilute solution.

hints: Identify the three corners of the cycle: solid $\text{AgNO}_3$, gaseous ions and aqueous ions.
Remember the direction of each arrow: solid to aqueous is solution, gaseous to solid is lattice formation, gaseous to aqueous is hydration.
walkthrough:
Place the three states**
Put the most separated state at the top: $\text{Ag}^+(\text{g}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{g})$. Put the dissolved state in the middle: $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{aq})$. The solid $\text{AgNO}_3(\text{s})$ sits at the bottom. Every species must show $(\text{s})$, $(\text{g})$ or $(\text{aq})$.

Draw the two downward arrows**
From gaseous ions down to solid is lattice formation, $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus$. From gaseous ions down to aqueous ions is the sum of the two hydration enthalpies. The upward or downward link between $\text{AgNO}_3(\text{s})$ and aqueous ions is $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^\ominus$. This closes the Hess triangle.

Final answer: Top level: $\text{Ag}^+(\text{g}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{g})$. Middle level: $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{aq})$. Bottom level: $\text{AgNO}_3(\text{s})$. Arrows: $\text{Ag}^+(\text{g}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{AgNO}_3(\text{s})$ ($\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus$), $\text{Ag}^+(\text{g}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{aq})$ (hydration), $\text{AgNO}_3(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}_3^-(\text{aq})$ ($\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^\ominus$), all with state symbols.

hints: Apply Hess law to the cycle: hydration sum equals lattice energy plus solution energy, then rearrange for $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus$.
walkthrough:
Substitute into the Hess expression**
Going from gaseous ions to aqueous ions directly equals going via the solid: $$\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}(\text{Ag}^+) + \Delta H_{\text{hyd}}(\text{NO}_3^-) = \Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus + \Delta H_{\text{sol}}^\ominus$$ So $$-475 + (-314) = \Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus + (+22.6)$$ Rearranging gives $$\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus = -789 - 22.6 = -811.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Final answer: $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus = -811.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Order the three nitrates by the charge on the cation first, since charge has the largest effect on lattice energy.
For the two $1+$ cations, $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Rb}^+$, compare their ionic radii down Group 1.
Link greater charge and smaller radius to stronger electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
walkthrough:
Put magnesium first**
Lattice energy depends on the attraction of $+$ for $-$. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ carries twice the charge of $\text{Na}^+$ or $\text{Rb}^+$, so it pulls $\text{NO}_3^-$ far more strongly. That makes formation of $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2(\text{s})$ from gaseous ions release the most energy, most exothermic.

Split sodium and rubidium by size**
Both are $1+$, so look at radius. $\text{Na}^+$ is above $\text{Rb}^+$ in Group 1, so $\text{Na}^+$ is smaller. The ion centres can approach closer, the charge density is higher, so $\text{NaNO}_3$ has a more exothermic lattice energy than $\text{RbNO}_3$.

State the electrostatic reason**
In words the examiner needs: larger ionic charge and smaller ionic separation mean stronger electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, stronger ionic bonding, and therefore a larger magnitude (more negative) $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^\ominus$.

Final answer: $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2(\text{s})$ most exothermic, $\text{NaNO}_3(\text{s})$, $\text{RbNO}_3(\text{s})$ least exothermic.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has a higher charge than $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Rb}^+$, and $\text{Na}^+$ is smaller than $\text{Rb}^+$.
Greater charge and smaller ionic radius give stronger attraction between ions / stronger ionic bonds, so more exothermic lattice energy.
